title: The 3pm crash has a cause, and it is findable
dek: Cortisol, blood sugar, and iron all show up in the afternoon. Here is how to tell which is yours.
description: The afternoon energy crash has three common causes that need different treatments. Dr. Nina Ross, ND PhD in Atlanta explains how to tell blood sugar, cortisol, and iron apart.

hero.alt: A woman working steadily through the middle of her afternoon
hero.caption: The afternoon is where most people first notice something has changed.

shortAnswer: An afternoon crash is usually blood sugar, cortisol, or iron. All three feel similar and need different fixes, so the useful question is which one, rather than how much more coffee.

body.text: It arrives somewhere between two and four. The screen stops making sense, your eyes get heavy, and the only plan available is caffeine or something sweet. An hour later you feel worse than before.

Most people file this under being busy. It deserves more than that, because an afternoon that falls apart on schedule is one of the most reliable signals your body sends, and it points at three things we can measure.
Blood sugar, and the shape of your morning

The most common version is a glucose curve with too much amplitude. A breakfast that was mostly carbohydrate takes you up quickly, insulin overcorrects, and the floor of that dip lands squarely in your afternoon.

The tell is timing tied to meals rather than the clock. You fade ninety minutes after eating, whenever you eat, and protein at breakfast changes the entire shape of the day. That is the cheapest experiment in this article.
An afternoon that falls apart on schedule is not a character flaw. It is a pattern, and patterns have causes.

The six numbers we read
When someone tells me their afternoon disappears, we look at these together:
Read together, these six numbers explain nearly every afternoon crash we see, and each one has a different first move.

body.caption: Glucose, insulin, cortisol, and ferritin on one page, read against each other.

body.text: Cortisol, and why the curve beats the number

Cortisol is supposed to peak in the morning and taper across the day. When that curve flattens or shifts, mornings feel like wading through water and the drop arrives early in the afternoon instead of at bedtime.

A single morning cortisol misses this entirely, because the shape is the finding rather than the value. We read it at four points, and where the pattern stays unclear we move to a full cortisol panel that maps the whole day at once.

body.text: Four days of writing down what you ate and when you faded will tell me more than most panels do.
Iron sits underneath both
Iron is the quiet one. Ferritin below about thirty will produce afternoon fatigue, breathlessness on stairs, and hair in the shower long before a standard blood count looks abnormal.
This gets missed constantly, because the complete blood count comes back normal and the conversation stops there. Ferritin is a separate request, and rebuilding it takes months rather than weeks.

body.caption: Most of the fix for the meal-linked version happens before nine in the morning.

body.text: What changes when we read it this way
Naming which of the three you are dealing with turns a vague complaint into something you can start on this week. Blood sugar responds in days. Cortisol takes a few weeks. Iron takes a season.
We retest at ninety days so the improvement is something you can see rather than something you are trying to remember, which matters most in the iron cases where the change is genuinely slow.
Where to start
Before your consult, write down what you ate and when you faded for four days. That alone separates the meal-linked pattern from the clock-linked one, and it costs nothing but a notes app.
Then we sit down for half an hour, put those four days beside your labs, and decide which of the three we are chasing first.

Cortisol has to be read as a curve across the day. One morning number hides the pattern.
Ferritin under thirty causes afternoon fatigue while a standard blood count still reads normal.
Protein at breakfast is the cheapest test here. Give it five days before you judge it.

title: Cortisol curves and why your afternoon matters
dek: One number at 8am hides the whole story. The curve is where the answer lives.
description: A single morning cortisol tells you almost nothing. Dr. Nina Ross, ND PhD in Atlanta explains how we read the cortisol curve across a day and what each shape means for your energy.

hero.alt: A woman finding calm after cortisol testing
hero.caption: Cortisol is a rhythm. Reading it once is like hearing one note.

shortAnswer: Cortisol is supposed to rise sharply on waking and taper all day. The shape of that curve explains your energy far better than any single value, and one morning draw cannot see a shape.

body.text: Cortisol has a bad reputation it partly deserves and mostly does not. It is the hormone that gets you out of bed, holds your blood pressure up, and keeps your blood sugar available. You would be in serious trouble without it.

The problem is never really the amount. It is the timing. Cortisol is meant to arrive in a particular pattern, and when that pattern shifts, you feel it in ways that look like a dozen unrelated complaints.
What cortisol is actually for
A healthy curve spikes within thirty minutes of waking, stays useful through the morning, drifts down across the afternoon, and reaches its floor around midnight so melatonin can do its job.
That morning spike is the part people lose first. Without it, waking feels like climbing out of wet sand no matter how long you slept, and the day never quite starts properly.
One cortisol at 8am is a single frame of a film. The plot is in the rest of the day.
One cortisol at 8am is a single frame of a film. The plot is in the rest of the day.
What we read to see the curve
To see a shape rather than a moment, we collect these:
Read together, these tell us the shape of your day rather than one moment in it.

body.alt: A four point cortisol panel being reviewed with a patient
body.caption: Four collections across one day, which is the only way a shape becomes visible.

body.text: The flat curve and the reversed one
The flattened curve is the most common pattern we see, and it is the one that produces the afternoon most people describe: a fog that arrives around two and lifts around six.

The reversed curve is harder to live with. Low in the morning, climbing in the evening, which is the physiology behind being exhausted all day and wide awake at eleven. Where sleep is the main complaint, the three in the morning pattern is worth reading alongside this.
body.html: The reversed curve is harder to live with. Low in the morning, climbing in the evening, which is the physiology behind being exhausted all day and wide awake at eleven. Where sleep is the main complaint, the three in the morning pattern is worth reading alongside this.

body.text: Tell me how the first thirty minutes of your day feel and I can usually guess the shape before we test.
Why the curve went sideways
None of this happens without a reason. Years of short nights, restriction, over-training, unmanaged inflammation, or a genuinely hard stretch of life all show up in this curve.
That is why we treat the reason alongside the pattern. Supplements aimed at cortisol while the cause continues will produce a few good weeks and then the same curve again.

body.alt: A calm morning routine that helps restore a healthy cortisol curve
body.caption: For a flattened curve, most of the repair happens in the first hour of the day.

body.text: What changes when we read the shape

Knowing which shape you have changes the plan immediately. The flat curve needs morning light, protein, and a training load that is not adding to the problem. The reversed one needs the evening handled first.
We retest at ninety days with the same four-point collection, and watching the curve steepen is one of the more satisfying things to show someone.
Where to start
Before your consult, note what time you wake, when you crash, when you get a second wind, and how you feel in the first thirty minutes of the day. That sketch usually predicts the result.
Then we sit down for half an hour, decide whether we need the panel or whether your pattern is already clear enough to start working on.

title: Reading ferritin the way we read it
dek: The number your doctor called fine is often the number behind your hair loss.
description: A ferritin of 18 gets called normal and still causes hair loss and fatigue. Dr. Nina Ross, ND PhD in Atlanta explains how we read iron stores and what it takes to rebuild them.

hero.alt: An iron panel laid out on a desk for review
hero.caption: One line on a panel, and one of the most useful lines we have.

shortAnswer: Ferritin is stored iron, and the lab range for it was built to catch anemia rather than to keep your hair. A reading in the teens is technically normal and functionally too low.

body.text: Ferritin is the number I get asked about least and think about most. It is your iron savings account, and almost everything your body treats as optional gets defunded when the balance runs down.

Hair is first in that queue. So is the energy you were counting on at four in the afternoon. Both of them go before a blood count shows anything at all, which is why so many people are told they are fine.
What ferritin actually measures
Most labs flag ferritin below about thirteen or fifteen. That threshold exists to catch iron deficiency anemia, which is a different and later problem than the one bringing you in.
A range built to catch disease is not the same as a range built for you to feel well. For hair specifically, the research and the clinic both point considerably higher than the bottom of that range.
Your body defunds your hair long before it lets your blood count slip. That order is the whole point.
Your body defunds your hair long before it lets your blood count slip. That order is the whole point.
What we read next to it
When ferritin comes back low, or suspiciously mid-range, we read these alongside it:
Read together, these tell us whether you are low, why you are low, and whether your body can absorb what we give you.

body.alt: A patient whose shedding resolved once her iron stores were rebuilt
body.caption: Regrowth follows iron, but it follows on iron time rather than ours.

body.text: Why the lab range is not the target

Iron does not exist on its own. Absorbing it needs stomach acid, and using it needs copper, vitamin A, and B12 in the picture. Inflammation quietly raises ferritin at the same time, which can mask a real deficiency.

That is why a single number gets read alongside the rest rather than acted on by itself, and why we look at inflammation markers in the same draw. If your gut is part of the reason, the gut panel usually explains it.
body.html: That is why a single number gets read alongside the rest rather than acted on by itself, and why we look at inflammation markers in the same draw. If your gut is part of the reason, the gut panel usually explains it.

body.text: A ferritin of eighteen is not a normal result. It is a warning somebody decided to round up.
Finding out why you are low
The other half of this is why. Heavy cycles, a vegetarian diet, low stomach acid, a gut that is not absorbing, or blood loss nobody has looked for. Iron deficiency is a symptom too.
Repleting without answering that question means doing it again in a year. We spend part of the consult on the cause, not just the correction.

body.alt: An intravenous iron session at the Atlanta studio
body.caption: Where absorption is the problem, we stop asking the gut to do the job.

body.text: What changes when we read it this way
When ferritin comes up, the order things return in is fairly consistent. Energy first, usually within weeks. Then the shedding slows. Then, months later, the regrowth you were actually hoping for.
That lag is worth knowing in advance, because month two feels like nothing is happening. Retesting at ninety days is what gets people through it, since the number moves before the mirror does.
Where to start
Ask for ferritin by name, and bring any old results you have. Three years of a slowly falling number tells us more than one reading in isolation ever could.
Then we sit down for half an hour, look at where you are and why, and decide whether this is oral iron, an IV, or a gut problem wearing an iron costume.

title: The four hormones we test when your cycle goes sideways
dek: Estrogen alone tells you very little. These four, read together, show the pattern.
description: Estrogen alone explains almost nothing. Dr. Nina Ross, ND PhD in Atlanta walks through the four hormones we read together when a cycle becomes unpredictable, heavy, or painful.

hero.alt: A woman tracking her cycle at home in a notebook
hero.caption: A cycle that changed has a reason, and the reason is usually measurable.

shortAnswer: A single estrogen reading pulled on a random day tells you almost nothing. We read estrogen, progesterone, and their two upstream signals across a timed window, because the ratio between them is what explains how you feel.

body.text: Your cycle used to be something you barely thought about. Now it arrives four days early or eleven days late, the first two days flatten you, and the week before it you do not recognise your own patience.
Somebody probably drew a single hormone level and told you it was fine. On a random Tuesday, in a system that changes every day of the month, one number was never going to answer this.
What one estrogen reading can tell you

Estrogen and progesterone move in a choreography, and the whole point is the relationship between them. Estrogen builds in the first half. Progesterone should rise and hold in the second half, after ovulation actually happens.

When progesterone comes in low or late, estrogen is unopposed for too long. That is the pattern behind heavy bleeding, breast tenderness, and the short fuse that arrives seven days before anything else does.
Hormones only make sense as a ratio. One number on one day is a snapshot of a moving thing.

The four we read together
When a cycle becomes unpredictable, heavy, or painful, we read these as one picture:
Read together, and read on the right day, these four turn an unpredictable month into something with a shape you can work with.

body.text: Why the day you test decides the answer

Timing is most of the accuracy here. Progesterone drawn on day three tells you nothing, because it has not happened yet. We aim for roughly seven days after ovulation, which for a lot of people is not day twenty-one at all.

That single correction changes results more often than any supplement. Before we treat anything, we make sure we tested when your body had something to show us, and where cycles are too irregular to time we use a urine panel instead that reads a whole month at once.

What sits underneath a cycle
A cycle that has changed is information rather than a verdict. Thyroid, iron, insulin, and cortisol all reach into it, which is why we run them alongside rather than after.

Chasing hormones on their own while a thyroid runs slow or ferritin sits at fifteen tends to produce a year of adjustments that never quite hold. Settling the surroundings often settles the cycle with very little else.

From there the plan is concrete, and we retest across a full cycle at ninety days so you can watch the second half fill in rather than guessing from how one week felt.

Track two cycles before your consult if you can, even roughly. Start day, how heavy, how you slept, when your mood turned. That timeline is genuinely diagnostic, and nobody else is going to ask you for it.
Then we sit down for half an hour, put your symptoms next to your dates, and decide which day of which week we are drawing blood.

title: GLP-1 done with your muscle in mind
dek: How we protect strength while the weight comes down, and why that decides whether it stays off.
description: A GLP-1 works, and what you lose alongside the fat decides whether it stays off. Dr. Nina Ross, ND PhD in Atlanta explains how we protect muscle through a weight loss program.

shortAnswer: A GLP-1 lowers appetite, and appetite is not selective. Without enough protein and enough resistance work, a quarter of what you lose can be muscle, and muscle is what keeps it off.

body.text: These medications work. That part is settled, and pretending otherwise is not useful to anyone sitting in front of me hoping for help.

What is not settled is how they get used. Mailed as a vial with a titration schedule and no other conversation, they produce weight loss that is partly muscle and rebounds the moment the prescription stops.
What these medications actually do
When you eat much less, your body takes some of what it needs from lean tissue. Studies of rapid loss without resistance training put that share somewhere around a quarter of total weight lost.
Muscle is where you burn glucose and where your resting metabolism largely lives. Losing it makes you smaller and slower at the same time, which is exactly the setup for regain.
Appetite suppression is not selective. Your body will take the muscle unless you give it a reason not to.

body.text: Protein first, and more than you think

That difficulty is the actual work of the program, and it is why we plan meals rather than hope. Where insulin resistance is the driver underneath, the insulin picture is worth understanding first.

body.text: Losing weight is the easy half now. Keeping the muscle while you do it is the part that needs a plan.
Load is the signal that saves muscle
Resistance training twice a week is the other half, and it does not need to be complicated or long. It needs to be heavy enough to give your body a reason to keep the tissue.
Walking is good for you and does not accomplish this. The signal that preserves muscle is load, and thirty minutes twice a week is enough to send it.

We retest at ninety days and track more than weight. Waist, strength, and body composition tell us whether the loss is the kind you want, and we adjust dose against that rather than against the scale alone.

Bring your labs, especially fasting insulin and A1c, and be honest about what you are eating now. The protein target is the hardest part and I would rather plan for that than discover it in month two.
Then we sit down for half an hour, look at whether a GLP-1 fits, and write the protein and training plan that goes with it before anything gets prescribed.

title: Your gut map, one marker at a time
dek: A plain-language tour of a stool panel and what each finding changes.
description: A GI-MAP result is intimidating until someone walks you through it. Dr. Nina Ross, ND PhD in Atlanta explains each marker in plain language and what each one changes about your plan.

hero.alt: A GI-MAP stool panel result laid out for review
hero.caption: Twelve pages of markers, and about six of them decide the plan.

shortAnswer: A gut panel looks intimidating and mostly is not. Six markers do the heavy lifting: digestive capacity, inflammation, the immune layer, the good bacteria, the opportunists, and the enzyme that recycles your estrogen.

body.text: A stool panel arrives as twelve pages of unfamiliar names and coloured bars, and almost everyone reacts the same way. They scan for anything in red, decide they are full of parasites, and arrive genuinely worried.
What a gut panel actually measures
These panels use PCR to count the DNA of what lives in your gut, alongside markers for how well you digest, how inflamed you are, and how your immune layer is holding up.

The counting part is impressive and also the part people over-read. A named organism at a low level is usually a normal resident rather than an invader, and treating every red bar is how people end up worse.
The value is in the interpretation, not the panel. The same twelve pages produce very different plans.
The value is in the interpretation, not the panel. The same twelve pages produce very different plans.
The six markers that decide the plan
Of everything on the report, six markers change what we actually do. The rest is context, useful for confirming a picture rather than driving a decision.

This is the part I wish more people knew before they pay for one of these: the value is in interpretation rather than in the panel. The same twelve pages produce very different plans depending on who reads them.

body.alt: A meal chosen to support digestion during gut repair
body.caption: Digestive capacity gets addressed before anything aimed at bacteria.

body.text: Digestive capacity comes before anything else
Pancreatic elastase tells us whether you are producing enough enzyme to break food down. When it is low, nothing downstream is going to work properly, and that becomes the first target.

Steatocrit tells us about fat digestion, which points at bile. Both of these come before anything aimed at bacteria, because feeding undigested food to a disturbed population makes the population worse. This is the bloating conversation in audio if you prefer.
body.html: Steatocrit tells us about fat digestion, which points at bile. Both of these come before anything aimed at bacteria, because feeding undigested food to a disturbed population makes the population worse. This is the bloating conversation in audio if you prefer.

body.text: Inflammation and the immune layer
Calprotectin measures inflammation in the gut wall directly, and it is the marker that decides whether we need to involve a gastroenterologist rather than proceeding alone.

Secretory IgA is your gut immune layer. Low means your defences are worn down, often after a long stressful stretch, and high means they are actively fighting something. Both change the order of treatment.

body.alt: A woman whose cycle settled once her gut was treated
body.caption: The estrogen recycling marker is where gut work and hormone work meet.

body.text: Please do not read your own report at midnight. Everything looks like a parasite at midnight.
The estrogen recycling marker
Beta-glucuronidase is the one nobody expects on a gut panel. It is the enzyme that unpackages estrogen your liver has already prepared for removal, sending it back into circulation.
High readings genuinely explain heavy cycles and breast tenderness, and they are invisible on a blood hormone panel. This is where gut work and hormone work turn out to be the same work.
What the first six months look like
The first six months follow a fairly consistent order: digestion first, then inflammation, then rebalancing the population, then rebuilding the lining, then a retest to see what actually moved.
We retest at ninety days for the markers we targeted, and the panel we compare against is your own previous one rather than a textbook, because your baseline is the only fair comparison.

title: The gut work that comes before everything else
dek: Hormones and energy both run through your gut. That is where most plans begin.
description: Hormones, thyroid, and energy all depend on your gut working. Dr. Nina Ross, ND PhD in Atlanta explains why gut repair comes first and what the first six weeks look like.

hero.alt: A meal being prepared at home with digestion in mind
hero.caption: Almost every plan we write starts within a few feet of the kitchen.

shortAnswer: Your gut absorbs the nutrients your thyroid needs, clears the estrogen your cycle depends on, and makes most of your serotonin. When it is struggling, everything downstream of it struggles too.

body.text: People come in to talk about their hormones, their hair, or their energy. We usually end up talking about their gut within the first ten minutes, and it is not a deflection.
Almost everything else in the body is downstream of digestion. Nutrients get absorbed there, hormones get cleared there, and a surprising share of your mood chemistry is manufactured there.
Why we start here
Thyroid hormone needs selenium, zinc, and iron to convert into its active form. Every one of those has to make it across your intestinal wall first, which is not guaranteed.
This is why thyroid plans stall. The prescription is right, the dose is right, and the raw material is not arriving. Fixing absorption often does more than adjusting the dose again.
Your thyroid prescription is only as good as the gut that has to deliver the raw material.

Read together, these show us what your gut is doing rather than what it feels like it is doing.

body.text: The estrogen loop nobody mentions
Estrogen gets used, then packaged by your liver, then carried out through your gut. Certain bacteria can unpackage it on the way and send it back into circulation.
That recycling is a real mechanism behind heavy cycles and tender breasts, and it is invisible on a blood hormone panel. If your cycle is the main complaint, the DUTCH panel shows this clearly.

What the first six weeks look like
The first six weeks rarely involve much that comes in a bottle. It is how you eat, how quickly, whether you are eating in the car, and whether your nervous system has left the office yet.
Digestion runs on the calm branch of your nervous system. Eating in a hurry means asking for stomach acid and enzymes at exactly the moment your body has decided they are not a priority.

body.caption: Fewer afternoon crashes is usually the first sign the gut is settling.

body.text: What changes when the gut settles
When the gut settles, the reports are consistent and quick: fewer afternoon crashes, calmer skin, a cycle that hurts less, and supplements that finally seem to do something.
That last one matters most. A working gut makes every other part of the plan cheaper and faster, which is why we spend the early weeks here rather than adding more.

Before your consult, track four days of food, timing, and symptoms, and note how long after eating things happen. Ninety minutes versus six hours points at completely different causes.
Then we sit down for half an hour, look at where digestion is breaking down, and decide whether we are testing or simply changing how you eat first.

title: Hormone restoration, titrated to you
dek: Why the dose that works for someone else is rarely the dose that works for you.
description: Hormone therapy works when the dose fits the person. Dr. Nina Ross, ND PhD in Atlanta explains how we test, titrate, and monitor hormone restoration rather than starting everyone the same.

hero.alt: A patient reviewing her hormone restoration plan
hero.caption: The right dose is found rather than chosen, and finding it takes a few months.

shortAnswer: Hormone therapy works when the dose fits the person. That means testing before you start, adjusting on how you feel and what your labs say, and accepting that the first dose is a starting point rather than an answer.

body.text: Two women the same age with the same symptoms can need doses that differ by a factor of three. That is not imprecision, it is biology, and it is the entire reason this has to be titrated.
How much you make, how fast you clear it, what your receptors do with it, and what else is going on all vary. A protocol that starts everyone in the same place will be wrong for most of them.
Why one dose does not fit
A pellet mill can only really offer one thing, so it offers that. Insert, wait months, repeat. If the dose was too high there is no taking it back, and if it was too low you wait.
That model exists because it is efficient, not because it is precise. What it removes is the ability to adjust, which is the part that actually makes hormone therapy work.
The first dose is a hypothesis. What makes this work is being willing to change it.

We monitor at ninety days indefinitely, because bodies keep changing and a dose that was right two years ago may not be right now.

title: How an IV drip earns its place in your plan
dek: What your labs have to show before we put anything in a bag.
description: An IV is a delivery method, not a treatment plan. Dr. Nina Ross, ND PhD in Atlanta explains what has to show up on your labs before a drip is worth doing, and what goes in it.

shortAnswer: An IV is a delivery route rather than a treatment. It earns its place when your labs show a real deficiency and your gut cannot absorb the oral version fast enough to matter.

body.text: Drips are everywhere now, sold by the menu and named after hangovers. That version is fine and mostly harmless, and it is a different thing from what happens here.

The question we ask before anyone sits in the chair is simple: what is low, why is it low, and is there a reason your gut cannot fix this with a capsule. If those three have answers, an IV is genuinely useful.
The question we ask first
Swallowing a nutrient and absorbing it are two different events. Between them sit stomach acid, bile, enzymes, an intestinal lining, and a bacterial population that may or may not be cooperating.

When any of that is compromised, oral doses go in and come out. That is the real argument for intravenous delivery: it skips a step that is not currently working, while we spend the rest of the plan repairing it.

A drip on its own does not change anything for long. It buys you a few weeks of feeling human while the slower work goes on underneath, and that is the honest way to describe it.
The slower work is the gut, the food, the sleep, and whatever was draining you in the first place. When we get that right, most people need fewer drips over time rather than more.

title: PCOS, and what we do in place of birth control
dek: A full walk through the testing, the food, and the plan that moves PCOS at the root.
description: Birth control masks PCOS symptoms without treating the insulin and androgen drivers underneath. Dr. Nina Ross, ND PhD in Atlanta explains the testing and the plan we use instead.

hero.alt: A woman managing PCOS with root-cause functional medicine care
hero.caption: PCOS is a metabolic condition wearing a reproductive costume.

shortAnswer: PCOS is driven by insulin and androgens far more often than by anything reproductive. Birth control quiets the symptoms while both drivers continue, which is why symptoms return the month you stop.

body.text: Most women arrive with the same story. Irregular cycles, weight that will not move, hair where they do not want it and thinning where they do. They were handed a prescription for the pill and told to come back when they wanted a baby.
What PCOS actually is

PCOS gets filed as a reproductive condition because of where the symptoms show up. Underneath, it behaves like a metabolic one: insulin resistance drives androgen production, and androgens interrupt ovulation.
That order matters enormously, because it means the leverage is metabolic. Treating the ovaries while insulin runs high is working at the wrong end of the chain.
PCOS is a metabolic condition that shows up in your cycle. Treat the metabolism and the cycle follows.
PCOS is a metabolic condition that shows up in your cycle. Treat the metabolism and the cycle follows.
The testing we run first
Diagnosis usually happens on symptoms and an ultrasound, which is a start rather than a finish. What we want is the mechanism, because the mechanism differs between women who share the same label.
Fasting insulin is the number most often missing, and it is frequently the whole story. Ask for it by name, because a normal glucose alongside high insulin is the classic PCOS pattern.

body.alt: A PCOS panel including fasting insulin and androgens
body.caption: Fasting insulin is the line most PCOS workups leave out and the one we start from.

body.text: Insulin is usually the engine
When insulin is high, your ovaries produce more testosterone. That is direct, well established, and it explains the acne, the hair, and the cycles that stopped arriving on schedule.

It also explains why weight loss feels impossible here rather than merely hard. High insulin blocks release, so effort produces very little, and the conclusion people draw is about themselves rather than about their physiology. The insulin explainer covers the mechanism in six minutes.

body.text: What we change about food
Food changes are the highest leverage thing available, and they are not a diet. Protein at every meal, carbohydrates paired rather than alone, and a genuine breakfast instead of coffee at eleven.
That combination lowers insulin within weeks, and lower insulin lowers androgens without a prescription. Most people notice skin and energy before their cycle changes.

body.text: You were not failing at weight loss. High insulin was holding the door shut the whole time.
The plan, in the order we build it

From there the plan stacks in order: food and movement, then targeted supplementation like inositol and magnesium, then medication where it earns its place, and hormone support only if the picture calls for it.
Birth control still has a role for some people, and choosing it with the mechanism understood is completely different from being handed it as the only option.
What the first year looks like
Cycles usually take three to six months to become predictable, because a follicle needs about ninety days to develop. Skin and energy move sooner, often in the first six weeks.
We retest at ninety days and track insulin, androgens, and cycle length together, because those three moving in the same direction is what tells us the root is actually shifting.

title: Peptides, explained plainly
dek: What they do in the body, who they suit, and how we dose them off your results.
description: Peptides explained without the hype: what they are, who they suit, and how Dr. Nina Ross, ND PhD in Atlanta prescribes and monitors them off your own lab results.

hero.alt: Prescription peptide therapy prepared in clinic
hero.caption: A real prescription, from a licensed pharmacy, dosed off a panel.

shortAnswer: A peptide is a short chain of amino acids that carries one specific instruction. That precision is the appeal, and it is also why the right peptide depends entirely on what your labs say.

body.text: Peptides arrived in the wellness conversation sideways, mostly through forums and gym conversations, which has left a lot of people with strong opinions and very little information.

The underlying science is neither new nor exotic. Insulin is a peptide. So is the GLP-1 everyone is currently talking about. What is new is how many of them we can now prescribe for specific, narrow jobs.
What a peptide actually is
Proteins are long chains of amino acids. Peptides are short ones, usually a few dozen at most, and being short makes them specific. Each one fits a particular receptor and delivers one message.

That message might be repair this tissue, calm this inflammation, release growth hormone in the pattern you had at thirty. The specificity is the point, and it is also the reason a peptide that helps one person does nothing for another.
A peptide carries one instruction. The whole question is whether your body needed that particular instruction.

The honest problem in this category is sourcing. Plenty of what gets sold online is labelled for research use, unverified, unregulated, and dosed by the buyer off a forum thread.

What we prescribe comes from a licensed compounding pharmacy, arrives with a certificate of analysis, and gets dosed off your panel with a physician monitoring it. If weight is the goal, the GLP-1 conversation is a more direct route than most peptides.

Why peptides come late in a plan
A peptide is not a starting point. It sits fairly late in a plan, after sleep, protein, iron, thyroid, and gut have been dealt with, because those four determine whether it can do anything at all.
Running a repair peptide while someone sleeps five hours a night is spending money to fight your own physiology. We get the foundation right first, which sometimes removes the need entirely.

We retest at ninety days, and cycling off is planned from the start rather than decided later.

Then we sit down for half an hour, look at whether a peptide has a job in your case, and if it does, which one and for how long.

title: Perimenopause, and what changes when you treat it early
dek: The window where small changes hold the most ground, and what we watch during it.
description: Perimenopause starts years before your last period and responds best when treated early. Dr. Nina Ross, ND PhD in Atlanta explains the timeline, the testing, and what to do first.

hero.alt: A woman in her forties feeling steady through perimenopause
hero.caption: The transition takes years, which is exactly why there is time to work with.

shortAnswer: Perimenopause begins years before your last period, and the early part is when the least effort buys the most. Sleep, bone, muscle, and mood are all easier to protect than to rebuild.

body.text: Almost nobody arrives here saying the word perimenopause. They arrive because sleep stopped working, or their cycle got strange, or their patience left the building sometime last spring and has not written since.
When perimenopause actually starts
Perimenopause is the transition, not the destination. It commonly begins in the early forties and can start in the late thirties, and it runs for four to ten years before periods stop entirely.
That length is the important part. This is not an event to get through in a bad season, it is a decade-long shift, and the early years are when intervention is cheapest and most effective.
Bone you keep is bone you never have to rebuild. That is the whole argument for starting early.
Bone you keep is bone you never have to rebuild. That is the whole argument for starting early.
The signs that arrive first
Sleep usually goes first, and it goes quietly. Progesterone is the calming hormone and the first to decline, so you fall asleep fine and wake at three, months or years before anything else changes.

Then cycles get shorter or heavier, the week before gets louder, and the word people use most often is that they do not feel like themselves. That sentence is a clinical finding as far as I am concerned.

body.alt: A hormone panel reviewed across a full cycle
body.caption: A month of data beats a single morning draw during a transition this variable.

body.text: What testing can and cannot tell you
Testing in perimenopause is genuinely tricky, and anyone promising a clean answer from one blood draw is overselling it. Hormones swing wildly month to month during this window.

What testing does do is rule things in and out, establish where you are, and give us a baseline to titrate against. For a fuller picture across a whole month, the DUTCH panel is more useful than a single draw.
body.html: What testing does do is rule things in and out, establish where you are, and give us a baseline to titrate against. For a fuller picture across a whole month, the DUTCH panel is more useful than a single draw.

body.text: Bone and muscle are the quiet stakes
Bone loss accelerates sharply in the years around your final period, and most of it happens quietly. There is no symptom until something breaks, which is why we do not wait for one.
Muscle goes the same way, and losing it changes your metabolism, your blood sugar, and how well you age in every direction. Protecting both now is enormously easier than rebuilding either later.

body.alt: A woman doing resistance training to protect bone and muscle
body.caption: Twice a week under load is the intervention with the longest payoff here.

body.text: Nobody comes in saying perimenopause. They come in saying they do not feel like themselves, which is the same sentence.
What we do in the early window

The early window is mostly unglamorous work: protein at every meal, resistance training twice a week, sleep treated as medical rather than optional, and hormone support if and when the picture calls for it.
What makes it worth doing early is compounding. Bone kept is bone you do not have to rebuild, and muscle kept is metabolism you do not have to fight for at sixty.
What the next ten years look like
Treated early, most people describe the next decade as an adjustment rather than a loss. Sleep holds, the cycle winds down without drama, and strength stays where it was.
We monitor every ninety days at first and then annually, watching bone density, body composition, metabolic markers, and how you actually feel, adjusting as your body keeps changing.

title: Sleep that finally holds through the night
dek: Waking at 3am is a signal. Here is what it usually points to.
description: Falling asleep fine and waking at 3am is a specific pattern with specific causes. Dr. Nina Ross, ND PhD in Atlanta explains what blood sugar, cortisol, and hormones do overnight.

hero.alt: A woman sleeping soundly through the night
hero.caption: Staying asleep and falling asleep are two different problems.

shortAnswer: Falling asleep easily and waking at three is a different problem from lying awake at eleven. The three in the morning version is usually blood sugar, cortisol, or falling progesterone.

body.text: You fall asleep without trouble. Then at some point between two and four you are awake, alert in a way that feels almost chemical, and the next ninety minutes belong to your inbox and your worries.
That specific timing is useful information. Trouble falling asleep and trouble staying asleep have different causes, and the middle of the night version narrows things considerably.
Why the time you wake matters
The most common driver is a blood sugar dip. If dinner was carbohydrate-heavy and early, glucose falls overnight, and your body wakes you with adrenaline to fix it.
The tell is waking with your heart going slightly faster than it should be, sometimes hungry, and settling if you eat something small. A protein-containing dinner often ends this within a week.
Waking at three with your mind already running is a different problem from waking hungry. The difference is the diagnosis.

What we read for overnight waking
For someone who falls asleep fine and wakes in the small hours, we read these:

body.text: Cortisol arriving too early
Cortisol should be at its lowest in the small hours. When the curve is disrupted, it climbs early, and you wake alert with your mind already running rather than groggy.
The distinguishing feature is mental rather than physical: thoughts arrive fully formed and urgent. Where this is the pattern, a four point cortisol panel shows the shape.

Progesterone and sleep that quietly stopped working
For women in their forties, falling progesterone changes sleep architecture directly. Progesterone is calming and it is the first hormone to decline in perimenopause.

The pattern is recognisable: sleep that worked for twenty years quietly stopped working, often alongside a cycle that has become less predictable. Sleep is frequently the first perimenopausal symptom, and rarely the one people mention.

body.caption: Sleep is often the first perimenopausal symptom and the last one people mention.

body.text: What changes when we name the mechanism
Naming the mechanism makes this fixable in weeks rather than years. The blood sugar version responds fastest, often within days of changing dinner.
We retest at ninety days, and honestly the better measure is that you have stopped knowing what your ceiling looks like at 3am.
Where to start
Track two weeks of when you wake, what you ate for dinner, and how you felt on waking, alert or groggy or anxious. Those three details usually identify the mechanism before any test does.
Then we sit down for half an hour, work out which one is yours, and start with dinner if that is where the evidence points.

title: Weight that will not move, and the six things we check
dek: When effort stops working, one of these six is usually holding the door shut.
description: When diet and exercise stop working, something measurable is usually in the way. Dr. Nina Ross, ND PhD in Atlanta walks through the six things we check before adding effort.

hero.alt: A patient walking as part of a weight plan
hero.caption: Effort was never the missing ingredient for most of the people we see.

shortAnswer: When effort stops producing results, something measurable is usually in the way. Insulin, thyroid, cortisol, hormones, iron, and sleep account for nearly all of it, and none of them respond to trying harder.

body.text: The people who come to us about weight are, almost without exception, the ones who have tried hardest. They have counted, walked, fasted, and cut. It worked once and stopped working.

Being told to do more of it is both exhausting and beside the point. If effort worked, you would not be reading this. So the useful question is what is standing in the way, and that is a question with measurable answers.
Why effort stopped working
High insulin is a storage signal. While it stays up, your body is not interested in releasing anything, regardless of how carefully you eat around it.
This is the most common finding on the list, and the one most often missed, because glucose can look perfect for years while insulin quietly climbs. It has to be asked for by name.
If effort were the missing ingredient, the people in my office would be the thinnest people I know.

The six we check
When a plan stalls despite real effort, we work through these six:
Read together, these six explain nearly every stalled plan we see, and each one has a different first move.

body.caption: Fasting insulin is the line most panels leave out and the one we start from.

body.text: Thyroid and cortisol, the two quiet ones
A slow thyroid lowers the rate at which you burn everything. Cortisol running high for a year holds fluid, drives cravings at night, and parks weight around the middle specifically.

Both of these are common in exactly the people who have been dieting hardest, because restriction and over-training are stressors themselves. Where the pattern points that way, the cortisol curve is where we look next.

body.text: You did not fail at this. Something measurable got in the way, and measurable things can be moved.
Sleep and iron belong on this list
Sleep is the one nobody wants on the list. Under six hours shifts the hormones that govern hunger and fullness within a couple of nights, and no amount of discipline outvotes that.
Iron belongs here too, quietly. Low ferritin means less oxygen carried, which means workouts that cost more and deliver less, and an afternoon with nothing left in it.

body.caption: Two nights under six hours changes appetite chemistry more than most diets do.

body.text: What changes when we read it this way

Naming which of the six is in your way usually replaces a year of guessing with one specific thing to correct. Insulin responds in weeks. Thyroid and cortisol take a couple of months. Iron takes a season.
We retest at ninety days, and the number on the scale is only one of the things we are watching. Waist, energy, and how your clothes fit often move first.
Where to start
Bring your old labs, even ones you were told were fine, and write down what you have already tried and how long each attempt lasted. That history is genuinely diagnostic.
Then we sit down for half an hour, put it all next to each other, and decide which of the six we are addressing before anything else gets added.
